title: What is Product Management?
snippet: Lesson 1: What is Product Management? Every discipline has a founding question. For Product Management, it is this: *if a PM doesn't write the code, doesn't design the interface, and doesn't manage the engineers as direct reports, what, precisely, are they accountable for?* Most people who enter Pro

title: Product Manager (PM)
snippet: The person accountable for deciding what a product should do and why, and for the fit between problem, solution, and business value.

title: Output
snippet: What a team produces or ships: a feature, release, or design change.

title: Outcome
snippet: The change in user or business behavior that results from an output.

title: Desirability
snippet: Whether users actually want a proposed solution.

title: Feasibility
snippet: Whether a proposed solution can realistically be built with available technology and resources.

title: Viability
snippet: Whether a proposed solution makes sense for the business, commercially or strategically.

title: Accountability Triangle
snippet: A framework stating that sound product decisions require desirability, feasibility, and viability simultaneously.

title: Decision Chain
snippet: A mental model tracing a product initiative through Problem → Understanding → Decision → Execution → Outcome, with feedback into the next cycle.

title: Build Trap
snippet: A pattern (named by Melissa Perri) in which teams measure themselves by output shipped rather than outcomes achieved.

title: Responsibility Without Authority
snippet: The organizational condition in which a PM is accountable for outcomes but lacks direct command authority over the people who produce them.

title: Project
snippet: A temporary endeavor with a defined scope and end date, producing a specific deliverable.

title: Product
snippet: An ongoing, evolving entity that serves a continuing user need for as long as that need exists and the business chooses to serve it.

title: Finite Work
snippet: Work with a defined win condition and endpoint; appropriately managed as a project.

title: Infinite Work
snippet: Ongoing work with no single win condition, only continued relative success or failure; appropriately managed as a product.

title: Iron Triangle (Project Management)
snippet: The traditional project-management framing of scope, schedule, and budget as the three variables under management tension. Distinct from Lesson 1's Accountability Triangle.

title: Product Thinking
snippet: The habit of examining the underlying user and business need behind a request before evaluating how to build a solution to it.

title: Root Cause
snippet: The underlying condition actually producing an observed symptom.

title: Product Lifecycle
snippet: Lesson 4: Product Lifecycle Lesson 2 established that a product has no natural finish line the way a project does. This lesson doesn't contradict that; it refines it. A product without a fixed end state can still move through recognizably different *stages*, each with different priorities, different

title: Product Lifecycle
snippet: The sequence of recognizable stages a product moves through (Problem-Solution Fit, Introduction, Growth, Maturity, Decline), each with distinct priorities.

title: Problem-Solution Fit
snippet: Evidence that a specific problem is significant for a specific group of people, and a proposed solution meaningfully addresses it for at least some of them.

title: Product-Market Fit (PMF)
snippet: Evidence that a solution works not just for early adopters but for a definable, reachable market at scale, typically signaled by strong organic retention and word-of-mouth growth.

title: Growth Stage
snippet: The lifecycle stage after PMF, where the primary challenge is scaling acquisition, activation, and retention efficiently.

title: Maturity Stage
snippet: The lifecycle stage where growth naturally slows due to market saturation; priorities shift to efficiency, defense, and adjacent opportunities.

title: Decline Stage
snippet: The lifecycle stage where usage or relevance is falling, requiring a deliberate decision to reinvest, harvest, or sunset.

title: User
snippet: The person who directly interacts with a product.

title: Customer
snippet: The person or entity that makes the purchasing decision and pays for a product.

title: User-Customer Alignment Spectrum
snippet: A model describing how closely user and customer interests overlap, from fully aligned to fully divergent.

title: Stakeholder Ledger
snippet: A practical habit of naming which stakeholder (user, customer, or both) a given request or signal represents before evaluating it.

title: Structural Bias (toward customer signal)
snippet: The organizational tendency to over-weight customer requests relative to user needs, because customer signal typically arrives through more powerful channels (sales, renewals).

title: Products for Dependents
snippet: Products where the user has no direct commercial relationship with the company (e.g., children's apps, pet trackers), and a guardian or customer makes product decisions on their behalf.

title: Job to Be Done (JTBD)
snippet: The underlying progress a person is trying to make in a given circumstance, independent of any specific product.

title: Laddering
snippet: The technique of repeatedly asking "why" or "what would that let you do" to decompose a stated request into its underlying job.

title: Functional Job
snippet: The practical task dimension of a job to be done.

title: Emotional Job
snippet: The dimension of a job concerned with how the person wants to feel while accomplishing it.

title: Social Job
snippet: The dimension of a job concerned with how the person wants to be perceived by others while accomplishing it.

title: Non-Consumption
snippet: The alternative of not solving a job at all, or solving it through an informal workaround, often a product's true largest competitor.

title: Forces of Progress
snippet: A model (Push, Pull, Anxiety, Habit) explaining why someone switches, or fails to switch, to a new solution.

title: Value Proposition

title: Table Stakes

title: Product Discovery
snippet: The process of testing assumptions and reducing risk in a proposed solution before committing to full-scale delivery.

title: Product Delivery
snippet: The process of designing, building, and shipping a validated solution at production quality and scale.

title: Value Risk
snippet: The risk that people will not actually want or choose to use/pay for a proposed solution.

title: Usability Risk
snippet: The risk that people cannot figure out how to use a proposed solution, even if they want its underlying value.

title: Feasibility Risk
snippet: The risk that a team cannot actually build a proposed solution within realistic technical, legal, or resource constraints.

title: Viability Risk
snippet: The risk that a solution does not work economically, legally, or strategically for the business, even if desirable and feasible.

title: Assumption Mapping
snippet: A technique for listing and plotting the assumptions a solution depends on, by confidence and importance, to find the riskiest one.

title: Discovery Theater
snippet: Activity that has the visible form of discovery but cannot produce disconfirming evidence, and therefore does not actually reduce risk.

title: Confidence Ladder
snippet: A sequence of progressively more expensive discovery tests (conversation, concept test, concierge test, limited pilot, full delivery), advanced one rung at a time.

title: Product Strategy

title: Diagnosis
snippet: An honest, evidence-based account of the actual situation and the real obstacle constraining progress.

title: Guiding Policy
snippet: The general logic or approach chosen to address a specific diagnosis, prior to specifying individual actions.

title: Coordinated Actions

title: The "Say No" Test

title: User Research
snippet: The disciplined, bias-aware collection and analysis of evidence about real users' behavior, needs, and context.

title: Qualitative Research
snippet: Research methods (interviews, observation) suited to why/how questions, with rich detail but small sample sizes.

title: Quantitative Research
snippet: Research methods (large-sample surveys, analytics, experiments) suited to how-many/how-much questions at scale.

title: Stated Preference
snippet: What a person says they want, believe, or would do, often in a hypothetical or low-stakes context.

title: Revealed Preference
snippet: What a person actually does when given a real opportunity, with real stakes, to act.

title: Confirmation Bias
snippet: The tendency to notice and weight evidence that supports an existing belief while discounting contradicting evidence.

title: Social Desirability Bias
snippet: The tendency for respondents to answer in ways that make them look good to the researcher, rather than reporting actual behavior or belief.

title: Evidence Trustworthiness Ladder
snippet: A ranking of research evidence by its resistance to bias, from weak (stated, unrepresentative, leading) to strong (revealed, representative, large-scale).

title: Survey

title: Survey Validity Chain

title: Customer Segmentation
snippet: The practice of dividing a user or customer base into meaningfully distinct groups relevant to product or business decisions.

title: Demographic/Firmographic Segmentation
snippet: Segmentation based on easily observable attributes (age, company size, industry), often weakly predictive of actual behavior unless validated.

title: Behavioral/Needs-Based Segmentation

title: Segmentation Validity Chain

title: Segmentation for Its Own Sake

title: Tactical Personalization Segmentation

title: Acceptance Criteria
snippet: The specific, testable conditions that define when a user story is complete.

snippet: A structured format for acceptance criteria: a precondition, a triggering action, and a specific, observable outcome.

title: Vanity Metric
snippet: A metric that looks encouraging and trends upward over time (such as cumulative signups) without indicating actionable product feedback or testing a clear hypothesis.

title: Actionable metric
snippet: A metric tied to a specific behavior a team could change, whose unexpected movement suggests where to investigate

snippet: A hidden variable that independently drives both of two correlated metrics, creating a false appearance of direct causation
